message.content: No, not in the standard probability sense. The reference question asks about discrete random variables X and Y. It asks whether E(X) and E(Y) can be finite while E(X + Y) is undefined or infinite. For a random variable, a finite expectation usually means absolute integrability. That means the expectation of the absolute value is finite. If E(X) is finite, then X is integrable. If E(Y) is finite, then Y is integrable. The sum of two integrable random variables is integrable. This follows from the triangle inequality for absolute values. The absolute value of X plus Y is bounded by the sum of their absolute values. The expectation of the sum of their absolute values is finite. Therefore the expectation of the absolute value of X plus Y is finite. So E(X + Y) exists and is finite. In that setting, linearity gives E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y). The discrete nature of X and Y does not change this conclusion. A countable sum definition of expectation still respects integrability. The only way to get trouble is if one uses a weaker or nonstandard notion of finite expectation. If conditional convergence is allowed, the phrase needs extra care. But under the usual definition, no such examples exist. The claimed undefined or infinite E(X + Y) cannot happen. The reason is that integrability is closed under addition. Thus the answer to the reference question is negative. No such discrete example exists and the short answer after checking the positive and negative parts of the expectation of both random variables and an integrability bound that follows from integration is hidden beneath the surface of the simple linearity rule.
